notes.meaning: Wisdom is described as a noble queen who has built a large, firm house. Carving out seven pillars shows that her home is completely built, strong, and beautiful. She has prepared a safe, welcoming place where people can come to learn and be protected.

differ.view: The house represents the church, and the pillars stand for the prophets, apostles, and ministers who support it.
The house is the church of Christ, and the pillars are faithful gospel preachers.
The seven pillars simply express the beauty, stability, and perfection of wisdom without requiring an elaborate allegory.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Early and medieval writers often viewed the house as Christ's human body and the seven pillars as the seven sacraments or the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit.

notes.meaning: Wisdom prepares a rich banquet with plenty of food and mixed wine. In Bible times, wine was mixed with water to make it suitable for drinking, or with spices to make it rich. She spreads her table generously so her guests can receive everything their souls need to thrive.

Wisdom sends out her servant girls through the city to deliver invitations. She also cries aloud herself from the highest, most visible places in town. Truth does not hide in dark corners; God makes His call open and clear to everyone.

Wisdom invites the simple and those who lack good judgment to come to her home. These are people who are young, inexperienced, or easily swayed, but still willing to listen. She does not call them to make fun of them, but to cure their ignorance and give them understanding.

Guests are welcomed to sit down and eat the bread and drink the wine Wisdom has prepared. Eating her feast means taking in God's word and letting divine truth feed the heart. Just as bread and drink nourish the physical body, God's wisdom gives true strength to the soul.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Ancient commentators took the bread and mixed wine as a direct prophecy of the bread and wine in the Lord's Supper.

notes.meaning: Wisdom requires her guests to leave their foolish ways and foolish friends behind. A person cannot enjoy a godly life while continuing to walk in harmful, sinful habits. Choosing understanding means turning away from wrongdoing and stepping onto the path that leads to life.

Trying to correct an arrogant scorner usually brings shame and insults back on the one speaking. A wicked mocker hates moral standards and will slander anyone who points out his faults. Knowing when someone refuses to listen saves us from useless arguments and personal abuse.

Do not waste rebukes on an obstinate mocker, or he will only turn around and hate you. On the other hand, if you gently correct a wise person, that person will love and thank you. Wise people appreciate correction because they want to please God and do what is right.

When you teach a wise person, that person welcomes the instruction and becomes even wiser. Righteous people never assume they have learned enough, so every piece of truth helps them grow. Humble hearts are always ready to increase their understanding.

True wisdom begins with the fear of the Lord, which is deep awe and reverence toward God. Real understanding comes from knowing the Holy One and what pleases Him. When a person starts with a humble respect for God, all other learning falls into its proper place.

Living by God's wisdom protects bodily health and can add years to a person's life. Following godly principles keeps people away from dangerous and wasteful sins that cut life short. It also points forward to the eternal life that God gives His people.

Each person must choose their own path and accept the result. If you choose wisdom, you yourself will gain the blessing, for God cannot be enriched by our good works. But if you mock God's truth, you alone will carry the guilt and suffer the consequences.

Here the writer pictures Folly as a loud, unruly woman who understands nothing good. Because she has no sound reasons or good gifts to offer, she relies on bold noise to draw attention. Her seductive words are meant to numb the conscience and pull people away from the truth.

Folly sits boldly by the door of her house, perched high up in the city like a queen on a throne. She does not do the hard work of preparing a feast like Wisdom did. Instead, she sits lazily in an important spot, pretending to have honor so she can lure victims inside.

Folly calls out to people who are simply walking by on their way to do their normal duties. She focuses on those who are headed in a straight, honest direction, trying to pull them off track. Temptation often works hardest against those who are seeking to live right.

Folly copies the exact words of Wisdom, shouting to the simple and those who lack judgment. She sets up her false school right along the street to confuse inexperienced people. Sin often imitates the sound of truth in order to make evil look harmless.

Folly tries to entice travelers by claiming that stolen water is sweet and secretly eaten bread tastes best. She plays on human curiosity and the sinful urge to break rules just because they are forbidden. She offers cheap bread and water disguised as an exciting, secret pleasure.

The victim who walks into Folly's house does not know that dead souls are already lying there. Those who give in to her trap end up in Sheol, the realm of the dead, separated from God and facing destruction. Sin promises hidden delight, but its final end is eternal ruin.
